title: How to Write a Thesis Statement

slides.notes: Thesis day. If all goes to plan, by the end of class every student has a strong, complex thesis statement and can begin actually writing. In pre-writing they went down into the mines, digging; today they come up with their treasure. Before you start, check student docs: anyone who still hasn’t found a specific focus may need a few more minutes of pre-writing on their diamond first.

runs.text: What details do you see in this picture?
Then: what’s going on in this picture?

slides.notes: "What’s happening in this picture?" again, same process as last time: first only what they SEE. An elephant; people up on store balconies; signs and advertisements; sacks of grain or rice in front; a man in a red and white turban; a cart with blue wire; something in the elephant’s rear (a dart?); a lamppost with exposed wires; motorcycles and bicycles; people running up stairs. Let them go, then ask what they think is going on. When students offer a theory, ask: "What do you see that makes you say that?" That is the observation-to-analysis move they will make in their thesis today. (The New York Times "What’s Going On in This Picture?" series has hundreds more of these.)

runs.text: This elephant wandered out of a forest and into the streets of a city in North Bengal, India, attacking houses, shops and vehicles over a period of hours. The elephant was finally calmed with three tranquilizer darts. The clash appeared to have a happy ending: the authorities said they returned the creature to the forest.
— Photo caption, The New York Times

slides.notes: Read the caption. Plenty of students guess India. Point out what they just did: observed details, then analyzed them into a theory. That is exactly what a thesis statement does.

Many students have never written an essay like this, so "thesis statement" may be an abstract idea to them. Don’t dwell on the definition; the examples will do the work.

runs.text: Everything else in the essay points back to it.

slides.notes: Go through these slides with the students. Have them read parts aloud if it keeps them engaged.

The number one problem with student thesis statements is that they are too general: "There are many themes in The Great Gatsby worth discussing." "Violence is a major problem in my community" is better but could be far more specific. Beware the 5-paragraph habit of three broad reasons; each of those is really its own essay. Specific is the goal.
See if students can define it before you show the next slide.

runs.text: Like the picture: what we see. Let’s look at some examples…

slides.notes: The next three observations are all real, from Brian’s students pre-writing on the prompt "What’s wrong with education today?" The first is Haley’s, whose sample essay you may have read with the class.

“Creative thinking is not prioritized in schools.”

slides.notes: Haley’s observation, from her pre-writing. Ask: is this true? If it reflects reality, it’s true.

slides.notes: Ask whether it reflects reality. Some kids will say "for some teachers, not for others." If it reflects reality somewhere, it’s true.

slides.notes: Does this reflect reality? Yes. So it’s true. All three are good observations.

runs.text: If I asked what’s happening in the picture and you just said “elephant, motorcycles, people,” I’d wonder what was wrong with you.

slides.notes: Think about the picture again. Calling out observations is not what I asked for; I asked you to analyze. Now let’s look at some analysis.

runs.text: Creative thinking is not taught enough in schools.
…this makes school boring for teachers and students

slides.notes: With "creative thinking is not taught enough in schools," the analysis we might offer: this makes school boring for teachers and students; it takes away motivation and excitement; they don’t feel as accomplished as they could if they were creating things.

runs.text: Most classroom teachers teach the way they were taught.
…this creates a situation where old ideas and methods are recycled, and new, current ideas are ignored

slides.notes: Second observation. Some analysis: old ideas and methods get recycled and new, current ideas are ignored; or simply, this is an ineffective teaching method. We could offer more; these are two examples.

runs.text: Schools place too much emphasis on right and wrong answers.
…this is a limited approach to learning
…it puts too much emphasis on correctness
…it ignores the personal expression of students’ experience

slides.notes: Third observation. This is a limited approach to learning; it puts too much emphasis on correctness; it ignores the personal expression of students’ experience. Again, there is more analysis available; these are the three we’ll use.

runs.text: On your document, create your own
Observation: Schools place too much emphasis on right and wrong answers.
• this is a limited approach to learning
• it puts too much emphasis on correctness
• it ignores the personal expression of students’ experience

slides.notes: Their observation is basically the specific topic they arrived at through pre-writing: "my essay is going to be about how schools place too much emphasis on right and wrong answers." Then 2–4 pieces of analysis: opinions, reactions, conclusions. Make sure everyone is on the "Thesis Statement" step at the top of the Tutor. Work the room; don’t sit down. The more specific they get, the better: we’re putting the topic under a microscope. Students sometimes think a long essay needs a big topic; it’s the opposite. Big and general makes a boring essay.

runs.text: Then combine them into your thesis

slides.notes: Today’s YAWP! editor on the Thesis Statement step, with a sample observation, analysis and thesis typed in. The Tutor’s instructions are on the left; when students have a draft thesis, they can ask the Tutor for feedback.

runs.text: COMBINE O & A TO FORM A THESIS
Creativity is not prioritized enough in schools.
…this makes school boring for teachers and students
When schools fail to prioritize creativity in teaching, school becomes boring for both students and teachers, resulting in a lack of shared motivation, excitement, and accomplishment.

slides.notes: Combine observation and analysis and you get the thesis from the sample essay. It’s all in there: every piece of the observation and analysis, in one sentence.

runs.text: COMBINE O & A TO FORM A THESIS
Most classroom teachers teach the way they were taught.
…this creates a situation where old ideas and methods are recycled, and new, current ideas are ignored
Teachers too often teach the way they were taught, which creates an ineffective learning environment where old ideas and methods are recycled, while new, current ideas are ignored.

slides.notes: Same move: teachers too often teach the way they were taught, which creates an ineffective learning environment where old ideas and methods are recycled while new, current ideas are ignored. One single complex sentence.

runs.text: COMBINE O & A TO FORM A THESIS
Schools place too much emphasis on right and wrong answers.
…this is a limited approach to learning
…it puts too much emphasis on correctness
…it ignores the personal expression of students’ experience

The education system’s obsession with testing represents a limited approach to learning that puts too much emphasis on right and wrong answers and ignores the personal learning experience of individual students.

slides.notes: And the third: the education system’s obsession with testing represents a limited approach to learning… It’s all in there. A beautiful, complex thesis statement.

After class, check every document for a working thesis; leave a positive comment, and where one is wordy or tangled, keep the original and add a "Revised thesis" below it so the student can see the difference. runs.text: It creates wordy situations. It’s a little word that needs other words to make it work. For example…

slides.notes: It isn’t that "to be" is never allowed. The problem is that it creates wordy situations, which is why some teachers ban it outright.
Three forms of "to be" in one sentence, and the sentence sags under them.

runs.text: Teacher training programs don’t emphasize creative design in lesson plans.
This is much better. It gives the sentence a stronger, more direct feel. This is called being
And being concise should be your goal in critical writing.

slides.notes: Editing "to be" out forces a rephrase. Read the new sentence aloud next to the old one and ask which sounds stronger.

runs.text: Creative design in lesson plans is really important and is something that isn’t taught in teacher training programs.
Teacher training programs don’t emphasize creative design in lesson plans.

slides.notes: Taking "to be" out forces a rephrase, and the result is stronger and more direct. This is called being concise, and concise should be the goal in critical writing.

slides.notes: The sentence is shorter now, and that is the point: there is space to say more.
